stem: In an armed conflict, an enemy fighter lays down his weapon and clearly surrenders. Under RA 9851, what is true about killing him?
choices: It is lawful, since he was a fighter earlier.
It is lawful if his unit is still fighting nearby.
It is a war crime, since he is hors de combat.
It is lawful if he had attacked civilians before.
answer: It is a war crime, since he is hors de combat.
hints: RA 9851 has a special term for a fighter who is out of the fight. What changes once he surrenders?
Recall Section 3(k), the meaning of "hors de combat". One of its cases is a person who "has clearly expressed an intention to surrender".
Then recall Section 4(c)(8), on killing or wounding a person known to be hors de combat. Check whether any excuse in the choices appears in it.

solution.methodName: Match the situation to the provision

steps.action: Spot the facts: the fighter laid down his weapon and clearly surrendered.
Section 3(k) of RA 9851 defines "hors de combat" to include a person who "has clearly expressed an intention to surrender".
steps.why: Hors de combat describes a person who is out of the fighting: captured, surrendered, or too wounded or sick to defend himself.

steps.action: Section 4(c)(8) lists as a war crime "Killing or wounding a person in the knowledge that he/she is hors de combat, including a combatant who, having laid down his/her arms or no longer having means of defense, has surrendered at discretion".
Section 4(c)(8) has no exception for what he did before, or for fighting that goes on nearby.
The answer is: it is a war crime, since he is hors de combat.

trapNotes.It is lawful, since he was a fighter ear: What matters is his status now. Once he clearly surrenders, he is hors de combat under Section 3(k), and killing him is a war crime under Section 4(c)(8).
trapNotes.It is lawful if his unit is still fighti: Section 4(c)(8) has no exception for fighting nearby. The person who surrendered is protected.
trapNotes.It is lawful if he had attacked civilian: Section 4(c)(8) has no exception for past acts. Killing a person known to be hors de combat is a war crime.
